the translocation of single-stranded RNA molecules through an idealized, cylindrical nanopore.
the translocation of structured polymers through a nanopore.
the anomalous scaling of the typical translocation times for structured heteropolymes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the scaling behavior of the typical translocation times for random RNAs is determined by their secondary structure properties and is not universal, but strongly depends on the sequence.
the scaling of the typical time with the sequence length in the molten and glassy phase is anomalous, and that it is not anomalous only in the molten but not in the glassy state.
the translocation time of a single RNA through a nanopore is typically not a simple power law in sequence length, but depends on the temperature and sequence length in a much more complex way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
translocation times for structured heteropolymetrs are typically much longer than those of unstructured polymers.

the anomalous scaling in translocation times of structured heteropolypeptides can be explained by the presence of a single dominant structure in the glassy case, whereas a large number of structures coexist in the molten case.
the translocation time of a structured RNA molecule through a nanopore depends on the sequence in a nontrivial way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
translocation through nanopores is a powerful technique to probe the structural properties of biomolecules.
the anomalous scaling of the translocation time is due to the fact that the polymer is not a single structure, but is rather a mixture of structures.
translocation of a structured RNA through a nanopore can be used as a sensitive probe of its secondary structure.
